The blocks are contiguous (each 8 fragments after the previous one), and the indirect block sits exactly between di_db[11] (29104) and logical block 12 (29120). That is the allocation policy written down in ffs_blkpref_ufs2: "The first indirect is allocated immediately following the last direct block and the data blocks for the first indirect immediately follow it" (ffs_alloc.c lines 1376-1385). Figure 7.3 compares this with a FAT chain.

Directories#

A UFS directory is also a file of entries, but the entries have variable length:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 7.16 – struct direct: variable-length directory entries in 512-byte chunks (dir.h lines 49-82)Source ↗
 * A directory consists of some number of blocks of DIRBLKSIZ
 * bytes, where DIRBLKSIZ is chosen such that it can be transferred
 * to disk in a single atomic operation (e.g. 512 bytes on most machines).
 *
 * Each DIRBLKSIZ byte block contains some number of directory entry
 * structures, which are of variable length.  Each directory entry has
 * a struct direct at the front of it, containing its inode number,
 * the length of the entry, and the length of the name contained in
 * the entry.  These are followed by the name padded to a 4 byte boundary
 * with null bytes.  All names are guaranteed null terminated.
 * The maximum length of a name in a directory is UFS_MAXNAMLEN.
 *
 * The macro DIRSIZ(fmt, dp) gives the amount of space required to represent
 * a directory entry.  Free space in a directory is represented by
 * entries which have dp->d_reclen > DIRSIZ(fmt, dp).  All DIRBLKSIZ bytes
 * in a directory block are claimed by the directory entries.  This
 * usually results in the last entry in a directory having a large
 * dp->d_reclen.  When entries are deleted from a directory, the
 * space is returned to the previous entry in the same directory
 * block by increasing its dp->d_reclen.  If the first entry of
 * a directory block is free, then its dp->d_ino is set to 0.
 * Entries other than the first in a directory do not normally have
 * dp->d_ino set to 0.
 */
#define DIRBLKSIZ       DEV_BSIZE
#define UFS_MAXNAMLEN   255

struct  direct {
        uint32_t d_ino;         /* inode number of entry */
        uint16_t d_reclen;              /* length of this record */
        uint8_t  d_type;                /* file type, see below */
        uint8_t  d_namlen;              /* length of string in d_name */
        char      d_name[UFS_MAXNAMLEN + 1];
                                        /* name with length <= UFS_MAXNAMLEN */

Each entry holds an inode number, its own record length, a type and the name with its length; the name can be up to 255 bytes. Directories are written in chunks of DIRBLKSIZ = 512 bytes (one sector, so a chunk is written atomically), and no entry crosses a chunk. The last entry of a chunk absorbs the free space through its d_reclen; deleting an entry adds its space to the previous entry's d_reclen. The root directory of the image:

Output 7.8 – The root directory of the official image, as stored (real; ufsx.py rootfs.img ls /)
directory inode 2, 512 bytes
offset    d_ino d_reclen  d_type d_namlen  d_name
     0        2       12     dir        1  .
    12        2       12     dir        2  ..
    24        3       20     reg        9  COPYRIGHT
    44        4       12     dir        3  bin
    56        5       16     dir        4  boot
    72        6       12     dir        3  dev
    84        7       12     dir        3  etc
    96        8       20     reg        9  firstboot
   116        9       12     dir        3  lib
   128       10       16     dir        7  libexec
   144       11       16     dir        5  media
   160       12       12     dir        3  mnt
   172       13       12     dir        3  net
   184       14       16     dir        4  proc
   200       15       16     dir        6  rescue
   216       16       16     dir        4  root
   232       17       16     dir        4  sbin
   248       18       12     dir        3  tmp
   260       19       12     dir        3  usr
   272       20      240     dir        3  var

Record lengths are the 8-byte header plus the name and a terminating NUL, rounded up to 4 (DIRECTSIZ, dir.h lines 105-112): 8 + 9 + 1 = 18, rounded to 20, for COPYRIGHT. var takes the remaining 240 bytes of the 512-byte chunk. Note what the directory does not contain: no size, no time, no attributes. Those belong to the inode, which is why one file can have several names (hard links): two entries holding the same inode number. Note also that the inode numbers are consecutive: this image was not written file by file by the kernel, but laid out in one pass by makefs(8) when the release was built.

How UFS2 chooses blocks#

ffs_alloc takes a preference (a block number near which to allocate) and falls back in a fixed order:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 7.17 – ffs_alloc: preferred block, same cylinder group, then rehash (ffs_alloc.c lines 130-148)Source ↗
/*
 * Allocate a block in the filesystem.
 *
 * The size of the requested block is given, which must be some
 * multiple of fs_fsize and <= fs_bsize.
 * A preference may be optionally specified. If a preference is given
 * the following hierarchy is used to allocate a block:
 *   1) allocate the requested block.
 *   2) allocate a rotationally optimal block in the same cylinder.
 *   3) allocate a block in the same cylinder group.
 *   4) quadratically rehash into other cylinder groups, until an
 *      available block is located.
 * If no block preference is given the following hierarchy is used
 * to allocate a block:
 *   1) allocate a block in the cylinder group that contains the
 *      inode for the file.
 *   2) quadratically rehash into other cylinder groups, until an
 *      available block is located.
 */

Directories are spread over the cylinder groups and files are kept near their directory (ffs_dirpref, ffs_alloc.c lines 1229-1240); a large file is moved to another group every fs_maxbpg blocks so that it does not fill one group (ffs_blkpref_ufs2, ffs_alloc.c lines 1376-1395). The 8% of space kept free (fs_minfree) exists so that the allocator always finds a good block nearby; only root can use it. Compare this with FAT's single next-fit cursor for the whole disk.

Soft updates, journaling and snapshots#

A UFS2 file system must also survive a crash. Creating a file changes at least four things: the inode bitmap in the cylinder group, the inode, the directory block, and the parent directory's inode. Early FFS wrote the metadata synchronously in a safe order, which was slow. Soft updates (newfs -U, the default for UFS2: newfs.c lines 391-393) keep the writes asynchronous but track the dependencies between buffers in memory, and when a buffer must be written before what it depends on, roll the unsafe change back in the copy being written:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 7.18 – Soft updates: dependencies, rollback and roll forward (softdep.h lines 43-62)Source ↗
/*
 * Allocation dependencies are handled with undo/redo on the in-memory
 * copy of the data. A particular data dependency is eliminated when
 * it is ALLCOMPLETE: that is ATTACHED, DEPCOMPLETE, and COMPLETE.
 *
 * The ATTACHED flag means that the data is not currently being written
 * to disk.
 *
 * The UNDONE flag means that the data has been rolled back to a safe
 * state for writing to the disk. When the I/O completes, the data is
 * restored to its current form and the state reverts to ATTACHED.
 * The data must be locked throughout the rollback, I/O, and roll
 * forward so that the rolled back information is never visible to
 * user processes.
 *
 * The COMPLETE flag indicates that the item has been written. For example,
 * a dependency that requires that an inode be written will be marked
 * COMPLETE after the inode has been written to disk.
 *
 * The DEPCOMPLETE flag indicates the completion of any other

The rules guarantee that the only inconsistencies a crash can leave are leaks: blocks and inodes marked in use that nothing references. A leak wastes space but cannot corrupt a file, so the system can mount the file system at once and fsck_ffs can reclaim the leaks later, in the background. Soft updates journaling (SU+J, newfs -j, which runs tunefs -j enable after mkfs, newfs.c lines 407-410) adds a small circular log of metadata operations in an inode named .sujournal; after a crash fsck_ffs replays the log instead of scanning the whole file system, which ffs(4) describes as reducing the time "from several minutes to a few seconds". Study case 7.B follows a file creation through a power failure on both systems.

Snapshots (mount -u -o snapshot, ffs_snapshot.c) freeze an image of a file system in a file inside it, using copy-on-write for blocks that change afterwards; dump -L and background fsck use them.

ZFS, briefly#

FreeBSD's other native file system is OpenZFS. It is not an evolution of UFS: it combines the volume manager and the file system, pools whole disks, never overwrites live data (every change is written to new blocks and a new root pointer is committed at the end, so the on-disk state is always consistent), checksums every block and can repair it from redundant copies, and makes snapshots and clones cheap. The installer offers ZFS or UFS; the VM images we use come in both flavours. This module stays with UFS2, whose on-disk format is small enough to decode by hand. The ZFS sources (sys/contrib/openzfs) are not part of the course's source checkout.

7.4 FAT and UFS2 compared#

The two formats answer the same questions in opposite ways. FAT keeps one global table for allocation and puts all other metadata in the directory entry; UFS2 keeps the metadata in an inode per file and splits allocation state into one bitmap per cylinder group.

Question FAT12/16 in MS-DOS 4.00 UFS2 in FreeBSD 15.1
Where is the list of a file's blocks? A linked list threaded through the FAT, one link per cluster (DOSSYM.INC lines 105-117) An array in the inode: 12 direct, 3 indirect pointers (dinode.h lines 121-163)
Unit of allocation Cluster of 2^n sectors, the same for every file 32 KB block; the last block of a small file can be 4 KB fragments (fs.h lines 122-139)
Free space FAT entries equal to 0; searched from a next-fit cursor (ROM.ASM lines 568-602) A bitmap of free fragments in each cylinder group (cg_freeoff, fs.h line 614)
Where is the metadata? Boot sector, FATs and root directory at the front; nothing elsewhere Superblock copy, bitmaps and inodes in every cylinder group
Per-file metadata 32-byte directory entry (DIRENT.INC lines 28-40) 256-byte inode; the directory entry has only name, inode number and type
File names 8 + 3 characters, upper case, padded with spaces Up to 255 bytes, any byte but / and NUL (dir.h lines 73-82)
Owner and permissions None; attribute bits read-only, hidden, system, archive di_mode (type and 12 permission bits), di_uid, di_gid, ACLs
Times Last write only, 2-second resolution, 1980-2107 Access, modify, change and birth time, 64-bit seconds plus nanoseconds
File size 32 bits (dir_size_l, dir_size_h) 64 bits (di_size); maximum fs_maxfilesize, about 2 PiB here
Hard links Impossible: the metadata is in the directory entry Several entries with one inode number; di_nlink counts them
Symbolic links None A file type; targets shorter than fs_maxsymlinklen (120 bytes) stored inside the inode (ufs_vnops.c line 2375)
Sparse files Impossible: every cluster up to the size is allocated Address 0 in di_db/indirect blocks means a hole that reads as zeros
Directory lookup Linear scan of 32-byte entries (DIR.ASM lines 86-140) Linear scan, or a hash table built in memory for large directories (Study case 7.C)
Finding byte n of a file Follow n / cluster size links from the first cluster At most 3 indirect blocks (Study case 7.A)
After a crash Nothing on disk says the volume is inconsistent; run CHKDSK by hand Soft updates allow only leaks; fsck_ffs in the background, or a journal replay with SU+J
Snapshots, quotas No Yes (ffs_snapshot.c, ufs_quota.c)

Two rows deserve a comment. Hard links are impossible on FAT not because of a missing feature but because of the design: if the size, first cluster and times are in the directory entry, two entries for one file would have two copies of each, and nothing could keep them equal. Unix put that metadata in the inode from the start, which made links, and the separation of "name" from "file", natural. Sparse files are a consequence of the pointer array: a block that was never written has no address, and the read path returns zeros for it. In a FAT chain every link must lead to the next cluster, so a file whose size says 1 GB has 1 GB of clusters.

FAT's strengths are real too. The format is tiny: Module 1 showed a boot sector that finds and loads IO.SYS in under 512 bytes, and a FAT12 reader in Python is a page of code. The metadata needs no interpretation of owners or permissions, so any system can read any FAT disk. It works on a 160 KB floppy. That is why the EFI system partition of the FreeBSD image (Output 7.1) is a FAT file system: firmware must be able to read it, and FAT is the format every firmware understands. It is FAT32, the 1996 extension that MS-DOS 4.00 cannot read: copied out with vhdpart.py ... 2 efi.img, its boot sector has the OEM name BSD4.4, the label EFISYS, 0 root directory entries and a 32-bit FAT size, and fatx.py says so and stops.

7.5 Disk access paths and caches#

MS-DOS: INT 21h, buffers, the driver and INT 13h#

A read on MS-DOS (Module 2, Study case 2.A) goes from INT 21h to the FAT code, which asks for sectors through the buffer pool configured by BUFFERS= in CONFIG.SYS (the lab image uses BUFFERS=20). Each buffer holds one sector and a header with the drive, the sector number and flags such as dirty and "this is a FAT sector" (BUFFER.INC lines 9-57). A dirty FAT buffer is written as many times as there are FAT copies (buf_wrtcnt, buf_wrtcntinc). Below the buffers, the kernel calls the block device driver in IO.SYS with a request header; the driver converts the logical sector to CHS and calls INT 13h; the BIOS programs the controller and waits. Whole-sector transfers of file data can bypass the buffers and go straight to the program's memory.

Programs can also skip the file system and call the kernel's sector layer directly with INT 25h (absolute read) and INT 26h (absolute write): drive number in AL, sector count in CX (or CX = -1 and a packet, section 7.2), buffer in DS:BX. DEBUG's L and W commands are thin wrappers:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 7.19 – DEBUG's L command is INT 25h with the 32-bit packet (DEBCOM2.ASM lines 1232-1258)Source ↗
;=========================================================================
; ABSREAD:      This routine performs a primitive logical sector read of
;               the specified drive.  This routine replaces the old
;               INT 25h function which only allowed 16 bit addressibility.
;               The new generic IOCtl logical sector read will permit
;               32 bit addressibility on a disk device.
;
;       Inputs : REL_READ_WRITE_TAB     - Table provides dword sector
;                                         addressibility.
;
;       Outputs: Data located at specified transfer address.
;
;       Error  : Carry is set on error.
;
;       Date      : 6/17/87
;=========================================================================

ABSREAD         proc    near            ;an000;read logical sector(s)

        push    ds                      ;an000;save affected regs
        push    cx                      ;an000;save affected regs
        push    bx                      ;an000;

        mov     cx,-1                   ;an000;extended format
        mov     bx,offset dg:rel_read_write_tab  ;an000;point to read/write table
        int     25h                     ;an000;invoke relative sector read
        pop     bx                      ;an000;discard stack word

Two quirks are visible here. INT 25h and INT 26h return with the caller's flags still on the stack (the handler ends with RET, not IRET, MS_CODE.ASM lines 127-193), so every caller must pop a word afterwards, as DEBUG does with pop bx ;discard stack word. And the write path, DSKWRITE, goes straight to the driver (DISK2.ASM lines 171-197): INT 26h invalidates the secondary cache and FASTOPEN's cache (MS_CODE.ASM lines 221-224) and marks the free count unknown, but it does not update or discard a buffer that already holds the same sector. If the kernel has a dirty copy of a FAT sector in a buffer and a program rewrites that sector with INT 26h, the kernel will later write its own copy over the program's. Nothing prevents a program from doing this to a disk with open files.

FreeBSD: the VFS, the buffer cache, GEOM and the driver#

On FreeBSD (Module 2, Study case 2.A) a read(2) goes through the VFS to ffs_read, which turns the file offset into a logical block number (lblkno) and asks the buffer cache for that block of the vnode with bread or cluster_read; only on a miss does the strategy routine translate the logical block to a disk address with ufs_bmaparray (ufs_vnops.c lines 2572-2573). FreeBSD's buffer cache is integrated with the virtual memory system: file data lives in pages of the vnode's VM object (the page cache), and buffers are mappings of those pages, "a coherent VM object and buffer cache scheme" (vfs_bio.c lines 35-36); metadata such as cylinder group and inode blocks is cached the same way through the device vnode, while indirect blocks are cached in the file's own vnode under negative logical block numbers (ufs_bmap.c lines 490-494). A miss becomes a struct bio sent to GEOM, which passes it down the stack of providers (ada0p4 to ada0) to the disk driver; the thread sleeps, the controller transfers by DMA, and an interrupt completes the request. Dirty buffers are written by the kernel's syncer within about 30 seconds (syncdelay, filedelay, vfs_subr.c lines 296-297), or at once by fsync(2); sync(2) asks every mounted, writable file system to start writing everything (kern_sync, vfs_syscalls.c lines 133-159).

Raw devices, and why writing under a mounted file system is dangerous#

On FreeBSD the raw disk is a file: dd if=/dev/md0 of=sector0 bs=512 count=1 reads its first sector, and dd the other way round writes it. Doing the second while the file system on md0 is mounted has the same problem as INT 26h on DOS, with more at stake: the kernel holds cached copies of superblock, cylinder group and inode blocks, and soft updates may be holding rolled-back versions of them; a block written behind its back will be overwritten later, or worse, mixed with cached state. GEOM therefore refuses it. When UFS mounts a provider read-write it opens it with read, write and exclusive access (g_access(cp, 1, wr, wr), geom_vfs.c line 297); opening /dev/md0 for writing later asks for write access (geom_dev.c lines 436-460) and g_access says no:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 7.20 – GEOM refuses a write open while someone holds exclusive access (geom_subr.c lines 1017-1025)Source ↗
                ;
        /* If we try exclusive but already write: fail */
        else if (dce > 0 && pw > 0)
                return (EPERM);
        /* If we try write but already exclusive: fail */
        else if (dcw > 0 && pe > 0)
                return (EPERM);
        /* If we try to open more but provider is error'ed: fail */
        else if ((dcr > 0 || dcw > 0 || dce > 0) && pp->error != 0) {

dd of=/dev/md0 on a mounted md0 thus fails with EPERM ("Operation not permitted"), and reading stays allowed. The flag G_F_FOOTSHOOTING (0x10 in the sysctl kern.geom.debugflags, geom.h line 251) disables the check for disks (geoms of rank 1, geom_subr.c lines 1015-1017), which is how one rewrites the boot code of a disk that is in use; its name says what the developers think of it. In the course VM (memory disk md17):

Output 7.9 – GEOM refuses to write under a mounted file system, unless told to shoot itself in the foot (captured in the course VM)
# mdconfig -a -t malloc -s 32m -u 17
# newfs -U /dev/md17 >/dev/null
# mount /dev/md17 /mnt
# geom md list md17 | grep Mode
   Mode: r1w1e1
# dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/md17 bs=512 count=1
dd: /dev/md17: Operation not permitted
# dd if=/dev/md17 of=/dev/null bs=512 count=1
1+0 records in
1+0 records out
512 bytes transferred in 0.000246 secs (2078766 bytes/sec)
# sysctl kern.geom.debugflags=16; dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/md17 bs=512 count=1; sysctl kern.geom.debugflags=0
kern.geom.debugflags: 0 -> 16
1+0 records in
1+0 records out
512 bytes transferred in 0.000218 secs (2350781 bytes/sec)
kern.geom.debugflags: 16 -> 0
# umount /mnt
# fsck_ffs -n /dev/md17
** /dev/md17 (NO WRITE)
** Last Mounted on /mnt
** Phase 1 - Check Blocks and Sizes
** Phase 2 - Check Pathnames
** Phase 3 - Check Connectivity
** Phase 4 - Check Reference Counts
** Phase 5 - Check Cyl groups
2 files, 2 used, 7813 free (21 frags, 974 blocks, 0.3% fragmentation)

Mode: r1w1e1 is the provider's acr, acw and ace of Listing 7.3: the mount holds one read, one write and one exclusive reference. The forced write did no harm only because it hit sector 0, inside the 64 KB that UFS2 leaves free in front of the superblock (SBLOCK_UFS2); a write at byte 65,536 would have overwritten the on-disk superblock behind the kernel's back. MS-DOS has no counterpart to any of this: any program can call INT 26h or INT 13h at any time.

7.6 The tools#

Task MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Create a scratch disk (a second floppy; dosb.py in the lab) mdconfig -a -t malloc -s 32m (mdconfig(8))
Partition FDISK (interactive, MBR only) gpart create -s gpt md0, gpart add -t freebsd-ufs md0
Make a file system FORMAT B: /V:LABEL [/S] newfs -U /dev/md0, newfs_msdos /dev/md1
Make a disk bootable SYS B:, FORMAT /S gpart bootcode -b /boot/pmbr -p /boot/gptboot -i 1 ada0
Volume label LABEL B:NAME, VOL tunefs -L name, glabel
Inspect the metadata CHKDSK /V, DEBUG L dumpfs, fsdb (read-only with -r)
Check and repair CHKDSK [/F], RECOVER fsck_ffs [-y], fsck_msdosfs
Change parameters (reformat) tunefs on an unmounted file system
Read a sector DEBUG L addr drive sector count dd if=/dev/md0 bs=512 skip=N count=1
Use the other system's disks No mount_msdosfs (msdosfs(4), Lab 7.7)

Three DOS tools are worth a closer look, because they show how much the format constrains them.

FORMAT /S and SYS. A system disk needs IO.SYS in the first root directory entry and in the first data clusters, at least its first three sectors contiguous (Module 0, section 0.4; Module 1). FORMAT /S writes them to an empty disk. SYS must add them to a disk that already has files, and DOS 4.00's SYS is much more willing to do this than earlier versions: it "will free up all required data clusters required by IBMBIO" and "will move entrys in order for IBMBIO and IBMDOS to be in their proper positions" (SYSHDR.INC lines 36-50). We ran SYS B: on the fragmented data disk of Lab 7.3, whose first clusters held K1.DAT (clusters 2-3) and FRAG.BAT (cluster 4), and whose first directory entry was the volume label:

Terminal
$ python labs/07-filesystems/dosb.py sys2.img "CTTY COM1" "SYS B:" "DIR B:"
$ python labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py sys2.img chain IO.SYS
Output 7.10 – SYS on a disk that was not prepared for it (real)
---- SYS B:
System transferred
---- DIR B:

 Volume in drive B is LAB7
 Volume Serial Number is 0C69-10F5
 Directory of  B:\

FRAG     BAT       290 04-25-24  12:00p
A        DAT      6144 11-09-26   9:11a
D        DAT      1024 04-25-24  12:00p
C        DAT      4096 11-09-26   9:11a
K1       DAT      1024 04-25-24  12:00p
        5 File(s)    1373696 bytes free

IO.SYS: first cluster 2, size 33321, 66 clusters (size needs 66)
chain: 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 16 -> 17 -> 18 -> 19 -> 20 -> ... -> 89 -> 90 -> 91 -> 92 -> FFFh
runs:  2-4, 16-20, 35-92  (3 fragments)
sectors of the first run: 33...35

SYS moved K1.DAT to clusters 13-14 and FRAG.BAT to cluster 15, moved the label and K1.DAT entries to the end of the directory, and wrote IO.SYS into clusters 2-4 and then wherever there was room. Exactly three clusters, sectors 33-35, are contiguous, because Free_Cluster computes how many clusters IBMLOADSIZE = 3 sectors need (SYS2.ASM lines 741-750); the loader in those sectors follows the FAT for the rest (Module 1). fatx.py check finds no problem with the result.

ATTRIB and hidden files. ATTRIB A:\IO.SYS answers "File not found - A:\IO.SYS": ATTRIB in 4.00 searches each directory with the attribute SUBDIR only (the value that carries the comment "Find all except volume labels" at ATTRIB.C line 2267), and then skips any entry with the hidden or system bit anyway (ATTRIB.C lines 2295-2304), so hidden and system files are never found, and the files it would be most interesting to look at are invisible to it. fatx.py ls shows them (RHS). CHKDSK counts them, and Lab 7.2 explains why it reports one more hidden file than there is.

DEBUG L and W. DEBUG reads and writes any sector with L address drive sector count and W address drive sector count (drive 0 = A:, numbers in hexadecimal). Lab 7.1 uses L; Lab 7.4 uses W to remove a volume label. RECOVER, which rebuilds a damaged directory by renaming every chain it finds to FILEnnnn.REC, is the most dangerous tool of the set and is not used in the labs.

On FreeBSD, newfs (newfs(8)) writes a superblock, its copies and empty cylinder groups; dumpfs prints them; fsdb is an interactive editor for inodes and directories (inode N, blocks, ls, fsdb(8)); fsck_ffs checks everything CHKDSK checks and more (link counts, inode types, bitmaps against the inodes); tunefs changes flags such as soft updates (-n) and journaling (-j) on an unmounted file system. Lab 7.5 uses all of them.

Labs#

The MS-DOS labs run on your computer with tools/dos_run.py and labs/07-filesystems/dosb.py; every output shown for them was captured on MS-DOS 4.00 built from source. Lab 7.3 and Lab 7.4 work on a second floppy image in drive B: so that the boot disk is never damaged; dosb.py writes to that image as a real drive would write to a diskette. The FreeBSD labs have two parts: steps in the FreeBSD 15.1 virtual machine, whose outputs were captured in the course VM (FreeBSD 15.1-RELEASE, 9 November 2026), and a static part on the real root file system of the official VM image, whose output is real too. In the course VM the memory disks were md17 and md18, because other experiments were using the machine at the same time; on your own VM the first memory disk is md0. All file names below are relative to the course repository; on Windows, write \ instead of / in paths given to Python if you prefer. Long command lines are wrapped for the page: type each $ command on one line. $L stands for labs/07-filesystems.

Lab 7.1: Sector 0 and the FAT with DEBUG#

Goal. Read the boot sector, a FAT sector and a root directory sector of the running system's own disk with DEBUG, and decode them by hand.

What you need. tools/dos_run.py; the script labs/07-filesystems/SECTORS.SCR.

Steps.

  1. Look at the script. L 100 0 0 1 loads (L) to offset 100h one sector from drive 0 (A:) starting at sector 0; D 100 L 40 dumps 40h bytes. All DEBUG numbers are hexadecimal, so sector 13h is sector 19.

    Example 7.1 – The DEBUG script (labs/07-filesystems/SECTORS.SCR)
    L 100 0 0 1
D 100 L 40
D 2F0 L 10
L 100 0 1 1
D 100 L 30
L 100 0 13 1
D 100 L 80
Q

  2. Run it on MS-DOS 4.00:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\SECTORS.SCR=labs/07-filesystems/SECTORS.SCR "DEBUG <SECTORS.SCR"

  3. In FreeBSD, attach the same floppy image and read the same sectors through the raw device (Module 0, section 0.6, shows how to copy the image into the VM):

    Shell
    mdconfig -a -t vnode -f /tmp/dos400.img -o readonly   # prints md0
dd if=/dev/md0 bs=512 count=1 2>/dev/null | hexdump -C | head -4
dd if=/dev/md0 bs=512 skip=19 count=1 2>/dev/null | hexdump -C | head -8
mdconfig -d -u 0

00000070  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 60  99 58 8d 00 b4 92 00 00  |.......`.X......|

The bytes are those of Output 7.11. Both dumps start at offset 0 because hexdump counts from the start of what it reads, and dd skip=19 hands it sector 19 alone; on the disk, the root directory starts at byte 2600h (19 x 512). Without 2>/dev/null, dd adds its "1+0 records in" summary to the screen.

What is going on. Sector 0 is the boot sector of Module 1: a JMP (EB 3C 90), the OEM name, and from offset 0Bh the BPB of Listing 7.4, little-endian. Reading it: 00 02 = 512 bytes per sector, 01 sector per cluster, 01 00 reserved sector, 02 FATs, E0 00 = 224 root entries, 40 0B = 2880 sectors, F0 media byte, 09 00 sectors per FAT, 12 00 = 18 sectors per track, 02 00 heads, 0 hidden and 0 big-total sectors, drive 00, 29h extended signature, serial 00 04 88 19 (= 19880400h, which DIR prints as 1988-0400), label and FAT12 . The sector ends with 55 AA. Sector 1 is the first FAT: entry 0 is FF0 (media byte F0h in the low byte), entry 1 is FFF, and from entry 2 on, 03 40 00 05 60 00 ... is the chain 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 … of IO.SYS (unpack it as in Study case 2.B). Sector 19 is the root directory: IO.SYS with attributes 07h (read-only, hidden, system), time 6000h (12:00:00), date 5899h (2024-04-25), first cluster 0002h and size 00008229h = 33,321 bytes; MSDOS.SYS starting at cluster 44h = 68; the volume label with attribute 08h; COMMAND.COM at cluster 8Dh = 141, 92B4h = 37,556 bytes. DEBUG reads these with INT 25h (Listing 7.19); the kernel's buffers are not involved.

Questions.

  1. Which BPB fields determine the first sector of the root directory and of the data area? Compute both from Output 7.11 alone.
  2. FAT entry 1 is FFF. Read the comment in DOSSYM.INC (Listing 2.19) and say what entries 0 and 1 are for. Why is entry 0 FF0 and not FF8 on this disk, and why will that matter in Lab 7.4?
  3. Change the script to dump the second FAT copy. Which sector do you load, and what do you expect to find?

Lab 7.2: A FAT12 explorer in Python#

Goal. Use fatx.py to read the lab image the way the kernel does, and check every number it prints against DIR and CHKDSK on the real system.

What you need. labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py, labs/07-filesystems/K1.DAT (a 1,024-byte text file).

Steps.

  1. Run commands on MS-DOS 4.00 that make a subdirectory and a file in it, and keep the disk afterwards:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\K1.DAT=labs/07-filesystems/K1.DAT --keep build/tmp/lab72.img
      "MD LAB7" "COPY K1.DAT LAB7\NOTES.TXT" "DIR LAB7" "CHKDSK A:"

  2. Explore the kept image:

    Terminal
    $ python labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py build/tmp/lab72.img info
$ python labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py build/tmp/lab72.img ls
$ python labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py build/tmp/lab72.img ls LAB7
$ python labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py build/tmp/lab72.img chain COMMAND.COM
$ python labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py build/tmp/lab72.img entry LAB7
$ python labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py build/tmp/lab72.img check

  3. Read fatx.py from Volume.read_bpb to Volume.entries. For each method, find the lines of the MS-DOS source it imitates; the docstring at the top lists them.

What is going on. fatx.py and CHKDSK agree on the free space (536 clusters, 274,432 bytes) and on the one directory of one cluster (512 bytes). The two system files take 66 + 73 = 139 clusters, 71,168 bytes, but CHKDSK counts three hidden files. The third is the volume label. In CHKDSK's first pass, an entry with the volume attribute skips the chain walk and jumps straight to the code that counts hidden files (TEST [SI.DIRATT],VOLIDA / JNZ $$IF29, and hidenfile: right after, CHKPROC.ASM lines 613-638), with a size of 0. DIR shows the dates of . and .. as the time MD ran (the emulator's clock), while NOTES.TXT keeps the date of K1.DAT: COPY copies the date and time of the source. fatx.py decodes the date with the bit layout of DIRENT.INC and prints the year in four digits; DIR prints two.

Questions.

  1. COMMAND.COM is 37,556 bytes in 74 clusters. How many bytes of its last cluster are unused? What would the waste be with the 8-sector clusters of a 10 MB hard disk partition?
  2. Why does .. in LAB7 hold cluster 0, and what would go wrong if MD wrote the root directory's first sector number there instead? (Hint: what is cluster 0 in the FAT?)
  3. fatx.py decides FAT12 or FAT16 from the cluster count. Make it print a warning when the BPB's file system id disagrees. Why is it right that the kernel does not trust that string?

Lab 7.3: Fragmenting a file on purpose#

Goal. Make MS-DOS 4.00 fragment a file, see the fragments with CHKDSK and fatx.py, and explain from the source why the same batch file gives two different layouts.

What you need. labs/07-filesystems/dosb.py, FRAG.BAT, K1.DAT and FMTANS.TXT (the answers to FORMAT's two questions: ENTER, then N).

Example 7.2 – Three files, delete the middle one, grow the first (labs/07-filesystems/FRAG.BAT)
@ECHO OFF
REM Lab 7.3: three files, delete the middle one, then grow the first
COPY /B K1.DAT+K1.DAT+K1.DAT+K1.DAT A.DAT
COPY /B K1.DAT+K1.DAT+K1.DAT+K1.DAT B.DAT
COPY /B K1.DAT+K1.DAT+K1.DAT+K1.DAT C.DAT
DEL B.DAT
TYPE K1.DAT >>A.DAT
TYPE K1.DAT >>A.DAT
COPY /B K1.DAT D.DAT
DIR

COPY /B with + concatenates in binary mode (without /B, COPY treats the sources as text and stops at a Ctrl-Z), so each of A.DAT, B.DAT and C.DAT is 4,096 bytes, 8 clusters. TYPE ... >>A.DAT appends 1 KB twice.

Steps.

  1. Run A: format a blank diskette in B:, put K1.DAT on it, make B: the current drive and run the batch file from drive A::

    Terminal
    $ L=labs/07-filesystems
$ python $L/dosb.py --new run-a.img --file A:\FMTANS.TXT=$L/FMTANS.TXT --file A:\K1.DAT=$L/K1.DAT
      --file A:\FRAG.BAT=$L/FRAG.BAT "FORMAT B: /V:LAB7 <FMTANS.TXT" "COPY K1.DAT B:\" "B:"
      "COMMAND /C A:\FRAG" "A:" "CHKDSK B:*.*"

  2. Run B: the same, but copy FRAG.BAT to B: as well and run it from there:

    Terminal
    $ python $L/dosb.py --new run-b.img --file A:\FMTANS.TXT=$L/FMTANS.TXT --file A:\K1.DAT=$L/K1.DAT
      --file A:\FRAG.BAT=$L/FRAG.BAT "FORMAT B: /V:LAB7 <FMTANS.TXT" "COPY K1.DAT B:\"
      "COPY FRAG.BAT B:\" "B:" "COMMAND /C FRAG" "A:" "CHKDSK B:*.*"

    (COMMAND /C runs the batch file in a second command interpreter, so that its output goes to the same place as the other commands' output.)

  3. Look at both disks: fatx.py run-a.img map, fatx.py run-b.img map, fatx.py run-b.img chain A.DAT.

Output 7.18 – The two disks seen by fatx.py: map of run A, then map of run B and chain A.DAT (real; one character per cluster, from cluster 2)
legend: . free  ? allocated in the FAT but in no file (lost)  ! in two files (cross-linked)
  A \K1.DAT
  B \A.DAT
  C \D.DAT
  D \C.DAT
    2 AABBBBBBBBBBBBCC..DDDDDDDD
legend: . free  ? allocated in the FAT but in no file (lost)  ! in two files (cross-linked)
  A \K1.DAT
  B \FRAG.BAT
  C \A.DAT
  D \D.DAT
  E \C.DAT
    2 AABCCCCCCCC........EEEEEEEECCCCDD
A.DAT: first cluster 5, size 6144, 12 clusters (size needs 12)
chain: 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 8 -> 9 -> 10 -> 11 -> 12 -> 29 -> 30 -> 31 -> 32 -> FFFh
runs:  5-12, 29-32  (2 fragments)
sectors of the first run: 36...43

What is going on. In run B, every disk access during the batch file is to drive B:: the batch file, K1.DAT and the new files are all there, and COPY, DEL and TYPE are built into COMMAND.COM. The floppy driver's door-latch logic (Listing 7.7) answers "not changed" to every media check, the DPB survives, and ALLOCATE continues from dpb_next_free (Listing 7.6): A.DAT gets 5-12, B.DAT 13-20, C.DAT 21-28; after DEL B.DAT, the appended clusters of A.DAT come from 29 onwards, not from the hole, and D.DAT follows at 33. In run A, COMMAND.COM reads the next line of FRAG.BAT from drive A: before every command (Module 3, section 3.6, describes how it reads a batch file one line at a time). Each access to B: then follows an access to another drive, the driver answers "don't know" (MEDIA$UNK, MSDISK.ASM lines 254-265 for drives without a change line, MS96TPI.INC lines 72-91 for drives with one), the kernel finds no dirty buffer for B:, treats the disk as new and rebuilds the DPB, which resets dpb_next_free to 0 (MISC.ASM lines 348-349). Every allocation therefore starts at cluster 2: A.DAT grows into the hole left by B.DAT, D.DAT fills most of the rest, and two clusters (18-19) stay free. CHKDSK B:*.* reports fragmentation with message 22 of CHKDSK.SKL ("%1 Contains %2 non-contiguous blocks").

Contiguity matters for speed because of OPTIMIZE: when a program reads many sectors, the kernel looks ahead in the FAT and gathers "the number of sequential sectors found so far" into one request to the driver (ROM.ASM lines 411-451). A contiguous file is read with one driver call per run (and the driver splits it per track); each extra fragment costs another request, a FAT lookup and, on a real drive, a seek of tens of milliseconds. The emulator does not model seek times, so you will not measure the difference here; on a 1988 floppy drive the run B layout of a large file could easily double its reading time.

Questions.

  1. Predict the map if run B is repeated with a fourth COPY to E.DAT (2 KB) added at the end of FRAG.BAT. Then predict it for a third run that boots again with the run B disk in B: and only copies E.DAT. Check both with dosb.py and fatx.py map.
  2. The comment in Listing 7.6 calls the search "towards higher numbered clusters" and explains a bug fixed at the boundary. What was the bug, and which line fixes it?
  3. FreeBSD's UFS2 would place A.DAT's new blocks very differently. Using Listing 7.17 and the comment of ffs_blkpref_ufs2, say where, and why the deleted B.DAT hole matters less there.

Lab 7.4: Breaking the FAT and letting CHKDSK find it#

Goal. Damage a FAT with Python in two ways, read CHKDSK's diagnosis, find every message and check in the source, and explain two surprises.

What you need. The run B disk of Lab 7.3 (copy it first: cp run-b.img lab74.img), fatx.py, and NO.TXT, YES.TXT and UNLABEL.SCR from labs/07-filesystems.

Steps.

  1. Make a lost chain: mark clusters 100 and 101 as a two-cluster chain that no file owns, in both FATs. Let fatx.py check describe the damage, then run CHKDSK without /F. CTTY COM1 sends all three standard handles to the captured output, because CHKDSK prints many messages to standard error, which dos_run.py does not capture on its own:

    Terminal
    $ python $L/fatx.py lab74.img setfat 100 101
$ python $L/fatx.py lab74.img setfat 101 0xFFF
$ python $L/fatx.py lab74.img check
$ python $L/dosb.py lab74.img --file A:\NO.TXT=$L/NO.TXT "CTTY COM1" "CHKDSK B: <NO.TXT"

  2. Add a cross-link: make the chain of D.DAT (33 -> 34) continue into the last clusters of A.DAT:

    Terminal
    $ python $L/fatx.py lab74.img setfat 34 31
$ python $L/fatx.py lab74.img check
$ python $L/dosb.py lab74.img --timeout 60 --file A:\NO.TXT=$L/NO.TXT "CTTY COM1" "CHKDSK B: <NO.TXT"

  3. Delete the volume label with DEBUG: load the first root directory sector of B: (drive 1, sector 13h), write E5h over the first byte of the label entry, write the sector back. Then run CHKDSK again, and once more with /F:

    Example 7.3 – Remove the volume label by hand (labs/07-filesystems/UNLABEL.SCR)
    L 100 1 13 1
D 100 L 20
E 100 E5
W 100 1 13 1
Q
    Terminal
    $ python $L/dosb.py lab74.img --timeout 150 --file A:\NO.TXT=$L/NO.TXT --file A:\YES.TXT=$L/YES.TXT
      --file A:\UNLABEL.SCR=$L/UNLABEL.SCR "DEBUG <UNLABEL.SCR" "CTTY COM1" "CHKDSK B: <NO.TXT"
      "CHKDSK B: /F <YES.TXT" "DIR B:"

What is going on. Step 1 is the textbook case: clusters 100-101 are marked in the FAT but MARKMAP never reached them from a directory, so CHKMAP flags them as orphans and FINDCHAIN counts one chain (CHKFAT.ASM lines 681-760). In step 3 with /F, the chain becomes FILE0000.CHK in the root directory, taking the first free slot (the label's, freed by DEBUG).

Step 2 is the first surprise. With a cross-link present, CHKDSK makes a second pass over all directories (CHKCROSS, CHKPROC2.ASM lines 231-249) and, for every entry that is not a directory, follows its chain again with CROSSLOOK. Unlike the first pass, the second pass does not skip volume labels (CHKPROC.ASM lines 596-603):

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 7.21 – CROSSLOOK: the second pass follows a chain until it reaches EOFVAL (CHKPROC.ASM lines 772-791)Source ↗
CROSSLOOK:
;Same as MRKFAT only simpler for pass 2
        MOV     [SRFCBPT],BX                               ;an014;bgb
        MOV     BX,SI                                      ;an014;bgb
        MOV     SI,[BX.DIRCLUS]                            ;an014;bgb
        CALL    CROSSCHK                                   ;an014;bgb
        JNZ     CROSSLINK                                  ;an014;bgb
;;;;;;;;mov     XA_Pass,False                              ;an014;bgb                      ;an014;bgb

CHLP:
        PUSH    BX                                         ;an014;bgb
        CALL    UNPACK                                     ;an014;bgb
        POP     BX                                         ;an014;bgb
        XCHG    SI,DI                                      ;an014;bgb
        CMP     SI,[EOFVAL]                                ;an014;bgb
        jae     chaindone                                  ;an014;bgb                      ;an014;bgb
;;;;;;;;JAE     Check_XA_Cross                             ;an014;bgb                      ;an014;bgb
        CALL    CROSSCHK                                   ;an014;bgb
        JZ      CHLP                                       ;an014;bgb
        JMP SHORT CROSSLINK                                ;an014;bgb

The label's first cluster is 0. UNPACK(0) returns FAT entry 0, which on this disk is FF0 (Output 7.11: media byte F0h). CROSSLOOK stops only at EOFVAL, FF8; FF0 is below it, so the loop treats FF0 as a cluster number, reads "FAT entry 4080" from memory past the end of the 2,849-entry FAT table, and keeps going through whatever it finds there. On our system it never came back. The kernel had exactly this problem and fixed it in 1986:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 7.22 – IsEof in the kernel: "Modified to accept 0FF0h as an eof" (FAT.ASM lines 77-91)Source ↗
Procedure IsEof,NEAR
        ASSUME  SS:DOSGROUP,CS:DOSGROUP,DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING
        Assert      ISDPB,<ES,BP>,"IsEOF"
        CMP     ES:[BP.dpb_max_cluster],4096-10 ; is this 16 bit fat?
        JAE     EOF16                   ; yes, check for eof there
;J.K. 8/27/86
;Modified to accept 0FF0h as an eof. This is to handle the diskfull case
;of any media that has "F0"(Other) as a MediaByte.
;Hopely, this does not create any side effect for those who may use any value
;other than "FF8-FFF" as an Eof for their own file.
        cmp     bx,0FF0h
        je      IsEOF_other
        CMP     BX,0FF8h                ; do the 12 bit compare
IsEOF_other:
        return

The fix never reached CHKDSK's second pass. The bug needs three things at once: a cross-link (otherwise there is no second pass), an entry with cluster 0 in some directory (a volume label or an empty file), and a media byte below F8h, which among standard formats means a 1.44 MB diskette (F0h). On a hard disk (F8h) FAT[0] is FF8, an end mark, and the loop stops at once. What happens after the loop leaves the FAT depends on memory contents past the table, so another machine may print nonsense instead of hanging. Removing the label (step 3) removes the cluster-0 entry and CHKDSK completes.

The second surprise is in the DIR listing: FILE0000.CHK is dated 11-09-94. CHKDSK builds the date of a recovered file itself, in Systime:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 7.23 – Systime packs the year with an 8-bit shift (CHKPROC2.ASM lines 370-379)Source ↗
        DOS_Call Get_Date                       ;                               ;AC000;
        SUB     CX, 1980
        MOV     AX, CX
        MOV     CL, 4
        SHL     AL, CL                          ; Push year to left for month
        OR      AL, DH                          ; move in month
        MOV     CL,4
        SHL     AX,CL                           ;Push month to left to make room for day
        SHL     AX,1
        OR      AL, DL

SHL AL, CL shifts the year (2026 - 1980 = 46 = 0101110b) left by 4 inside the 8-bit register AL, so its top bits fall off; only 46 AND 0Fh = 14 survives, and 1980 + 14 = 1994. The code is correct only for 1980-1995; the shift should have been on AX. When this CHKDSK was written, that was seven years away.

Notice also what /F did not do. The cross-link is reported but left alone, and D.DAT still has a 4-cluster chain for a 1,024-byte size (fatx.py check still reports both): Check_Chain_Sizes skips cross-linked files (CHKPROC.ASM lines 1543-1554). The user must copy both files elsewhere, decide which one is damaged, and delete the bad one.

Questions.

  1. Find the text of every message in Outputs 7.19-7.21 in USA-MS.MSG and the code that prints it. Which messages go to standard error, and how can you tell from CHKMSG.INC?
  2. Instead of removing the label, which other change to the disk would let CHKDSK finish while keeping the cross-link? Try it.
  3. Write the one-line fix for Systime and the one for CROSSLOOK. For the second, there are two reasonable places; which is safer?

Lab 7.5: Building and reading a UFS2 file system#

Goal. Create a UFS2 file system on a memory disk, look at it with dumpfs and fsdb, and decode the same structures yourself with ufsx.py, first on the official VM image and then on your own file system.

What you need. The FreeBSD 15.1 VM; labs/07-filesystems/mkufs.sh; on your computer, vhdpart.py, ufsx.py and the VM image download FreeBSD-15.1-RELEASE-amd64-ufs.vhd.xz (Module 0, section 0.6).

Steps.

  1. In the VM, as root, run the script, which makes a 32 MB memory disk, creates a file system with soft updates, adds a few files and prints what the tools see:

    Example 7.4 – A UFS2 file system on a memory disk (labs/07-filesystems/mkufs.sh)
    #!/bin/sh
# Lab 7.5: a UFS2 file system on a 32 MB memory disk, and what the tools say about it.
# Run as root in the FreeBSD 15.1 VM:  sh mkufs.sh 2>&1 | tee mkufs.out
set -e
md=$(mdconfig -a -t malloc -s 32m)            # prints the new unit, e.g. md0
echo "memory disk: /dev/$md"
diskinfo -v "/dev/$md" | head -4
newfs -U "/dev/$md"                           # UFS2, soft updates, 32 KB blocks, 4 KB fragments
dumpfs -m "/dev/$md"                          # the newfs command that would recreate it
dumpfs "/dev/$md" | head -20                  # superblock fields
mount "/dev/$md" /mnt
mkdir /mnt/dir
echo hello > /mnt/dir/small.txt
dd if=/dev/random of=/mnt/big.bin bs=1k count=100 2>/dev/null
ln /mnt/dir/small.txt /mnt/hardlink.txt
ln -s dir/small.txt /mnt/symlink
ls -lia /mnt /mnt/dir
ino=$(stat -f %i /mnt/big.bin)                # fsdb -r refuses "cd" (see the text): use the number
umount /mnt
fsdb -r "/dev/$md" <<EOF
ls
inode $ino
blocks
quit
EOF
dd if="/dev/$md" of=/tmp/ufs32.img bs=1m 2>/dev/null   # keep a copy for ufsx.py on your computer
mdconfig -d -u "${md#md}"
echo "image saved in /tmp/ufs32.img"

  2. On your computer, copy the root partition out of the VM image (about two minutes) and decode it:

    Terminal
    $ python labs/07-filesystems/vhdpart.py FreeBSD-15.1-RELEASE-amd64-ufs.vhd.xz 4 rootfs.img
$ python labs/07-filesystems/ufsx.py rootfs.img sb
$ python labs/07-filesystems/ufsx.py rootfs.img cg 0
$ python labs/07-filesystems/ufsx.py rootfs.img namei /etc/rc.conf
$ python labs/07-filesystems/ufsx.py rootfs.img inode 1108
$ python labs/07-filesystems/ufsx.py rootfs.img cat /etc/rc.conf

  3. The script left a copy of the memory disk in /tmp/ufs32.img. Copy it to your computer (scp, or python tools/bsd_run.py --get /tmp/ufs32.img:ufs32.img) and run ufsx.py on it: sb, cg 0, ls /, inode N for the numbers ls -i printed, and blocks /big.bin. Compare every field with dumpfs and fsdb.

Every field agrees with dumpfs: the id 6af19cd5 4ed0c074, 4 groups of 2,056 fragments and 1,152 inodes, dblkno 112, metaspace 80, maxcontig 32. The free counts differ from the dumpfs header only because dumpfs ran before the files were created (4,604 free inodes then, 4,600 after dir, small.txt, big.bin and symlink). ufsx.py inode 4 prints di_gen 0x64b97d68 and di_blocks 200, fsdb prints GEN=64b97d68 and BLKCNT=c8: the same numbers, fsdb printing them in hexadecimal (fsdbutil.c line 188).

What is going on. Cylinder group 0 of the official image is full: no free blocks, 49,854 free inodes. This image was not filled by the kernel, which would have spread directories over the nine groups with ffs_dirpref (ffs_alloc.c lines 1229-1240), but laid out in one pass by makefs(8) at release time: all 2,359 directories are in group 0, and the inode map starts with ff ff ff ff, every inode in a row in use. Inode numbers follow the same order: /etc is inode 7, right after /dev, and its files around 1,033-1,500. The firstboot file in the root directory and growfs_enable="YES" in rc.conf tell the first boot to grow the file system to the size of the virtual disk. dumpfs -m shows the result. In the course VM we ran it on the official root partition (the first 32 MB of rootfs.img, copied into the VM and extended to 5 GiB with truncate; dumpfs reads only the superblock and the summary area) and on the VM's own root file system after the first boot:

Output 7.25 – dumpfs -m on the official root partition and on the grown root of the VM (captured in the course VM)
# dumpfs -m rootfs.img
# newfs command for rootfs.img (rootfs.img)
newfs -L rootfs -O 2 -U -a 2 -b 32768 -d 32768 -e 8192 -f 4096 -g 16384 -h 64 -i 8192 -k 0 -m 8 -o time -s 10485760 rootfs.img
# dumpfs -m /dev/gpt/rootfs
# newfs command for /dev/gpt/rootfs (/dev/gpt/rootfs)
newfs -L rootfs -O 2 -U -a 2 -b 32768 -d 32768 -e 8192 -f 4096 -g 16384 -h 64 -i 8192 -k 0 -m 8 -o time -s 39763328 /dev/gpt/rootfs
# dumpfs /dev/gpt/rootfs | grep ^ncg
ncg     31      size    4970416 blocks  4814399

growfs changed only the size: 10,485,760 sectors (5 GiB) became 39,763,328 (19 GiB) and 9 cylinder groups became 31; block size, inode density (-i 8192, one inode per 8 KB of data) and the other parameters stay those of the image. fsdb and ufsx.py compute an inode's address with the same macros (Listing 7.13): inode 1108 is in group 1108 / 80256 = 0, inode block (1108 mod 80256) / 128 = 8 at fragment 40 + 8 x 8 = 104, slot 1108 mod 128 = 84, byte 104 x 4096 + 84 x 256 = 447,488.

Your own file system differs from the official one in four parameters, because newfs and makefs(8) choose different defaults; dumpfs -m turns the superblock back into a command line (dumpfs.c lines 428-470). newfs sets -a 32 (fs_maxcontig = MAXPHYS / block size, mkfs.c lines 245-246) where makefs sets -a 2 (64 KB / block size, ffs.c lines 359-361); it sets -e 4096 where makefs sets -e 8192 (the most blocks a file takes from one group before moving on: newfs divides the block size by the 8 bytes of a UFS2 block pointer, newfs.h line 66, makefs still by 4, under the comment "XXX ondisk32", ffs.c lines 362-364); it reserves 80 fragments per group for metadata (-k 80, "reserve half of minfree for metadata blocks", mkfs.c lines 458-463); and it turns on check hashes for the superblock, cylinder groups and inodes (mkfs.c lines 503-517), which the official image does not have (fs_metackhash 0x0 in Output 7.5). Because of the metadata area, the data of a group starts at fragment 112 + 80 = 192, which is exactly where big.bin begins, while the root directory's fragment, 120, lies inside the metadata area. newfs also made /.snap, inode 3, group operator, mode 775, the place for snapshots (mkfs.c lines 968-984). The inode numbers show the kernel's policy at work: big.bin (4) and symlink (5) are in group 0 with the root, but dir is inode 3456 = 3 x 1152, the first inode of cylinder group 3, and small.txt (3457) was put next to its directory (question 3 asks why). hardlink.txt shares inode 3457 with dir/small.txt, link count 2. big.bin's 102,400 bytes are three 32 KB blocks and one 4 KB fragment: fsdb prints the run lbn 0-3 blkno 192-216, and BLKCNT=c8 (200 sectors of 512 bytes = 3 x 32 KB + 4 KB); ufsx.py shows the short last block.

The script uses inode N and not cd big.bin, and for a reason we found the hard way. With cd, fsdb -r answers fsdb: `cd' requires write access and blocks then lists the root directory. cd and lookup are read-only commands, flagged FL_RO | FL_ST in fsdb's command table (fsdb.c lines 188-189), but FL_ST ("resplit final string") is defined as 0x0003, the bits of FL_WR and FL_CWR together:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 7.24 – fsdb's command flags: FL_ST overlaps the two write flags (fsdb.h lines 48-51)Source ↗
#define FL_RO   0x0000          /* for symmetry */
#define FL_WR   0x0001          /* wants to write */
#define FL_CWR  0x0002          /* wants to write critical data */
#define FL_ST   0x0003          /* resplit final string if argc > maxargc */

The command loop refuses every command with one of the write bits when the file system was opened with -r (fsdb.c lines 300-302). A flag that should have had a bit of its own (0x0004) turns two harmless commands into "write" commands: a one-character bug that has nothing to do with file systems and everything to do with bit masks.

Questions.

  1. From Output 7.5, compute how many bytes of the 5 GiB partition are inode tables, and what fraction of the disk that is. What newfs option changes it, and what does the man page newfs(8) say about it?
  2. Inode 1034, /etc/aliases, is a symbolic link of 12 bytes with di_blocks = 0. Where is its target stored? Run ufsx.py rootfs.img inode 1034.
  3. All 2,359 directories of the official image are in cylinder group 0. Would the kernel have placed them there if the same files had been created one by one on a mounted file system? Re-read the ffs_dirpref comment (ffs_alloc.c lines 1229-1240) and explain.

Lab 7.6: One file, two file systems#

Goal. Store the same 1 KB file on FAT and on UFS2 and compare, byte for byte, the metadata each needs.

What you need. The run B disk of Lab 7.3; the VM with the file system of Lab 7.5, attached again from its copy and mounted (mkufs.sh detached the memory disk at the end): mdconfig -a -t vnode -f /tmp/ufs32.img (prints md0) and mount /dev/md0 /mnt; K1.DAT copied into the VM.

Steps.

  1. On your computer: python labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py run-b.img entry K1.DAT and python labs/07-filesystems/fatx.py run-b.img fat 0 8.
  2. In the VM: cp K1.DAT /mnt/k1.dat; touch -t 202404251200 /mnt/k1.dat; ls -li /mnt/k1.dat; stat -x /mnt/k1.dat, then umount /mnt and run fsdb -r /dev/md0 with the commands ls, inode N (N from ls -i), blocks and quit, typed at its prompt or piped in with printf. fsdb starts at the root directory; do not use cd, which fsdb -r refuses (Lab 7.5).
  3. On your computer, run ufsx.py rootfs.img inode 1108 and ufsx.py rootfs.img ls /etc to see the same structures for a file of similar size in the official image.
