regular file, size 1024
        lbn 0 blkno 217

k1.dat got inode 6, the next free inode of group 0, mode 0644 (from the umask 022), owner root, di_size 1024 and one 4 KB fragment (BLKCNT=8, eight sectors). The fragment is 217, in the same 32 KB block as the last fragment of big.bin (216): before it breaks up a free block, ffs_alloccg looks for a run of free fragments in partly used blocks (ffs_alloc.c lines 1824-1838). The new directory record took the free space at the end of the root directory's chunk: the record of symlink shrank from 420 bytes (Output 7.23) to the 16 it needs, and k1.dat's record holds the other 404 (Listing 7.16). Only one of the four times is the time of the copy. touch -t set the access and modification times, and the kernel moved the birth time back with them: when the new modification time is earlier than the birth time, setutimes sets the birth time too, so that no file is modified before it was created (vfs_syscalls.c lines 3321-3330). The change time, set by the kernel on every inode change, is the only one that shows when the file arrived.

What is going on. On FAT the whole description of K1.DAT is 32 bytes in the directory and 3 bytes of FAT (two 12-bit entries, 2 -> 3 -> FFF) in each of two copies. The name and the metadata are one record: renaming rewrites the record, and there is no way to give the file a second name. On UFS2 the directory record is 16 bytes and holds only the name and the inode number; the inode holds 256 bytes, most of them for features FAT lacks (owner, group, mode, four 64-bit times with nanoseconds, generation number, flags, 15 block pointers). Allocation is one bit in the inode map and one bit (one fragment) in the free-fragment map of the cylinder group. Space is also used differently: the 1,024-byte file takes two 512-byte clusters on the floppy, and the 82-byte rc.conf takes one 4 KB fragment on UFS2.

Questions.

  1. Make a table of the bytes of metadata each system writes to create the file, counting both FAT copies and the inode, bitmap bits and directory record. Which writes must reach the disk before which for the file system to stay consistent after a crash (Study case 7.B)?
  2. In the VM, ln /mnt/k1.dat /mnt/k2.dat. What changes in the inode and in the directory? Why can no FAT tool do the same?
  3. touch -t set the modification time. Which of the four UFS times can a user set, and which only the kernel? (utimes(2), and di_birthtime.)

Lab 7.7: The DOS disk on FreeBSD: what msdosfs makes up#

Goal. Mount the MS-DOS floppy image on FreeBSD and find out where the owner, group, permissions, link count and inode number that ls -li prints come from, since FAT stores none of them.

What you need. The VM, the floppy image build/images/dos400.img copied to /tmp, labs/07-filesystems/msdosls.sh.

Steps.

  1. Run the script, which mounts the image read-only twice, first with the defaults, then with -u 1001 -g 1001 -m 644, and lists a few files with ls -lio each time:

    Example 7.5 – Owners and modes on msdosfs (labs/07-filesystems/msdosls.sh)
    #!/bin/sh
# Lab 7.7: what msdosfs reports for files that have no owner, group, mode or inode number.
# Run as root in the FreeBSD 15.1 VM, with the lab floppy image copied to /tmp/dos400.img.
set -e
md=$(mdconfig -a -t vnode -o readonly -f /tmp/dos400.img)
ls -ld /mnt                                   # the mount point supplies the defaults
mount_msdosfs -o ro "/dev/$md" /mnt
ls -lio /mnt/IO.SYS /mnt/MSDOS.SYS /mnt/COMMAND.COM /mnt/CONFIG.SYS
umount /mnt
mount_msdosfs -o ro -u 1001 -g 1001 -m 644 "/dev/$md" /mnt
ls -lio /mnt/IO.SYS /mnt/MSDOS.SYS /mnt/COMMAND.COM /mnt/CONFIG.SYS
umount /mnt
mdconfig -d -u "${md#md}"

  2. Read msdosfs_getattr (Listing 7.25) and match every column of the output with a line of it.

What you should see. With /mnt owned by root:wheel with mode 755, as in a fresh VM:

Output 7.29 – sh msdosls.sh (captured in the course VM)
drwxr-xr-x  2 root wheel 512 Jun 12 10:29 /mnt
307 -rwxr-xr-x  1 root wheel uarch                37556 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/COMMAND.COM
308 -rwxr-xr-x  1 root wheel uarch                   40 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/CONFIG.SYS
304 -r-xr-xr-x  1 root wheel hidden,rdonly,system 33321 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/IO.SYS
305 -r-xr-xr-x  1 root wheel hidden,rdonly,system 37376 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/MSDOS.SYS
307 -rw-r--r--  1 1001 1001 uarch                37556 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/COMMAND.COM
308 -rw-r--r--  1 1001 1001 uarch                   40 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/CONFIG.SYS
304 -r--r--r--  1 1001 1001 hidden,rdonly,system 33321 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/IO.SYS
305 -r--r--r--  1 1001 1001 hidden,rdonly,system 37376 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/MSDOS.SYS

ls sorts its operands, so COMMAND.COM comes first. User and group 1001 need not exist: the numbers are printed as they are. Directories get the same mask as files when -M is not given (mount_msdosfs.c lines 165-168), so with -m 644 a directory loses its execute bits. In the course VM, ls -ld /mnt on the second mount printed drw-r--r-- 1 1001 1001 7168 Jan 1 1980 /mnt (the root directory has no date of its own), and cat /mnt/CONFIG.SYS run as user 1001, the owner, failed with "Permission denied"; root, whose privilege overrides the mode, could still read the file.

What is going on. The owner, group and mask are properties of the mount, not of the files: mount_msdosfs fills in the owner, group and mode of the mount point directory when you do not give them (mount_msdosfs.c lines 196-207), and the kernel answers every stat(2) with them:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 7.25 – msdosfs_getattr: permissions, owner and flags made up from the mount and the DOS attributes (msdosfs_vnops.c lines 283-312)Source ↗
        mode = S_IRWXU|S_IRWXG|S_IRWXO;
        if (dep->de_Attributes & ATTR_READONLY)
                mode &= ~(S_IWUSR|S_IWGRP|S_IWOTH);
        vap->va_mode = mode &
            (ap->a_vp->v_type == VDIR ? pmp->pm_dirmask : pmp->pm_mask);
        vap->va_uid = pmp->pm_uid;
        vap->va_gid = pmp->pm_gid;
        vap->va_nlink = 1;
        vap->va_rdev = NODEV;
        vap->va_size = dep->de_FileSize;
        fattime2timespec(dep->de_MDate, dep->de_MTime, 0, 0, &vap->va_mtime);
        vap->va_ctime = vap->va_mtime;
        if (pmp->pm_flags & MSDOSFSMNT_LONGNAME) {
                fattime2timespec(dep->de_ADate, 0, 0, 0, &vap->va_atime);
                fattime2timespec(dep->de_CDate, dep->de_CTime, dep->de_CHun,
                    0, &vap->va_birthtime);
        } else {
                vap->va_atime = vap->va_mtime;
                vap->va_birthtime.tv_sec = -1;
                vap->va_birthtime.tv_nsec = 0;
        }
        vap->va_flags = 0;
        if (dep->de_Attributes & ATTR_ARCHIVE)
                vap->va_flags |= UF_ARCHIVE;
        if (dep->de_Attributes & ATTR_HIDDEN)
                vap->va_flags |= UF_HIDDEN;
        if (dep->de_Attributes & ATTR_READONLY)
                vap->va_flags |= UF_READONLY;
        if (dep->de_Attributes & ATTR_SYSTEM)
                vap->va_flags |= UF_SYSTEM;

The only per-file inputs are the DOS attributes: read-only removes the write bits; read-only, hidden, system and archive also become the BSD file flags rdonly, hidden, system and uarch that ls -lo prints (names from fflagstostr, strtofflags.c lines 59-83). The link count is always 1. The "inode number" is made up too: for a file it is the position of its directory entry, counted in 32-byte entries from the start of the disk (msdosfs_vnops.c lines 264-281). The root directory starts at sector 19, 16 entries per sector, so IO.SYS (entry 0) is 19 x 16 = 304 and COMMAND.COM (entry 3, after the label) is 307. Rename a file to another directory and its "inode number" changes.

None of this is visible to programs as a difference in system calls. truss cat /mnt/CONFIG.SYS on the msdosfs mount and truss cat config.sys on a copy of the file on UFS (both with the output sent to /dev/null) printed 72 lines each, identical except for the file name and addresses; the end of the first:

Output 7.30 – The last lines of truss -o truss-msdos.txt cat /mnt/CONFIG.SYS >/dev/null (captured in the course VM)
openat(AT_FDCWD,"/mnt/CONFIG.SYS",O_RDONLY,00)   = 3 (0x3)
copy_file_range(0x3,0x0,0x1,0x0,0x7fffffffffffffff,0x0) ERR#22 'Invalid argument'
fstat(1,{ mode=crw-rw-rw- ,inode=21,size=0,blksize=4096 }) = 0 (0x0)
read(3,"FILES=20\r\nBUFFERS=20\r\nDEVICE"...,4096) = 40 (0x28)
write(1,"FILES=20\r\nBUFFERS=20\r\nDEVICE"...,40) = 40 (0x28)
read(3,0x4d4bea42f000,4096)                      = 0 (0x0)
close(3)                                         = 0 (0x0)
close(1)                                         = 0 (0x0)
_exit(0x0)
process exit, rval = 0

cat first tries copy_file_range(2), which refuses a device as output, then falls back to read and write, on msdosfs exactly as on UFS. The 40 bytes of the DOS CONFIG.SYS, with their \r\n line ends, arrive through the same read(2); FAT, clusters and made-up inode numbers all live below the VFS.

Questions.

  1. With the image mounted read-write as user 1001 (-u 1001 -m 755), what happens on chmod 444 f, chmod 644 f and chown 0 f? Read msdosfs_setattr (msdosfs_vnops.c lines 326-516).
  2. Why is the made-up inode number based on the directory entry's position and not on the file's first cluster? (Hint: what is the first cluster of an empty file?)
  3. MS-DOS has no counterpart to -u and -m. Which DOS 4.00 mechanism comes closest to protecting files from other users, and how weak is it?

Study cases#

Study case 7.A: Finding byte 100,000 of a file#

Goal. Count the work each file system does to find one byte in the middle of a file, with real files.

The FAT file. On a data diskette in B: we made a 112,668-byte file with COPY /B COMMAND.COM+COMMAND.COM+COMMAND.COM B:\BIG.DAT on MS-DOS 4.00. fatx.py chain shows 221 clusters in two runs, 13-20 and 35-247 (the first run is the hole left by B.DAT in Lab 7.3). With 512-byte clusters, byte 100,000 is in the cluster with index 100,000 / 512 = 195 of the chain, at offset 160. To find it, the kernel starts at dir_first (13) and follows 195 links: 13 -> 14 -> … -> 20 -> 35 -> … -> 222. Each link is a FAT12 lookup (UNPACK, Study case 2.B) costing a few dozen instructions while the FAT sector is in a buffer; the 1.44 MB FAT is 9 sectors, so with BUFFERS=20 it can stay in memory, but on a 32 MB FAT16 hard disk partition with 2 KB clusters the FAT is 64 sectors and a long walk keeps replacing buffers. Cluster 222 is sector (222 - 2) x 1 + 33 = 253.

MS-DOS avoids most walks with a cache of one position: the SFT remembers the last cluster used and its index in the file (sf_lstclus, sf_cluspos), and FNDCLUS starts from there when the target is at or after it (ROM.ASM lines 84-114). Sequential reading therefore costs one link per cluster; a backward seek, or the first access after opening, restarts from the first cluster. The fast-seek part of FASTOPEN, new in 4.00, is a resident cache of cluster numbers that the kernel consults before walking the FAT (FastSeek_Lookup in FNDCLUS and OPTIMIZE, ROM.ASM line 125, ROM.ASM line 464).

The UFS2 file. On the root file system of the official image, /boot/kernel/kernel has 32 KB blocks. Byte 100,000 is in logical block 100,000 / 32,768 = 3, at offset 1,696: di_db[3] = fragment 29040 (Output 7.7), read directly from the inode. Byte 29,000,000 is in logical block 885, which is past the 12 direct blocks: ufs_getlbns (Listing 7.15) finds one level of indirection, entry 885 - 12 = 873 of the indirect block at fragment 29112, which holds fragment 36104; the byte is at offset 320 of that block. At most one extra block read, and usually none, since the indirect block is cached after the first use.

Byte FAT12, 512-byte clusters FAT16, 32 KB clusters UFS2, 32 KB blocks
100,000 195 links 3 links di_db[3], no extra read
29,000,000 56,640 links 885 links 1 indirect block
1,000,000,000 (larger than any FAT12 volume) 30,517 links 2 indirect blocks (double indirect)
2^40 (1 TiB) impossible impossible 3 indirect blocks (triple indirect)

What to notice. FAT's cost grows linearly with the position, and only caching (the SFT position, FASTSEEK, buffers) hides it; random access to large files on FAT is slow by construction. UFS2's cost grows with the logarithm of the position, base 4,096, and never exceeds three extra reads. The price is paid elsewhere: every file has a 256-byte inode, and a file between 384 KB and 128 MB needs one 32 KB indirect block of metadata.

Discussion questions.

  1. Compute the FAT16 numbers in the table for a volume with 2 KB clusters. Which cluster size makes FAT16 walks as short as possible, and what does it cost in wasted space for small files?
  2. A program reads a FAT file backwards, one cluster at a time from the end. How many links does MS-DOS follow in total for a file of n clusters?
  3. ext2 on Linux and UFS2 both use 12 direct pointers. What fraction of the files in /etc of the official image need an indirect block? (Use ufsx.py ls and inode, or write a loop.)

Study case 7.B: Power loss while creating a file#

Goal. Follow the writes that create a small file on each system and see what a power failure at each point leaves behind.

FAT. To create and write NEW.DAT (one cluster), MS-DOS changes three kinds of sectors: the root directory sector that receives the entry, one FAT sector in each of the two copies, and the data sector. The order in which they reach the disk is the order in which the buffers are flushed (the kernel writes a dirty buffer when it needs the buffer for something else, when the file is closed, or on INT 21h function 0Dh), not an order chosen for safety. Four cases:

Written before the power fails State after reboot Found by
Nothing Old state; the file never existed nothing to find
FAT only Clusters allocated that no entry references CHKDSK: lost clusters
Directory entry only An entry pointing to a cluster the FAT says is free CHKDSK: "Allocation error, size adjusted" or an invalid cluster
Directory and FAT, not the data A valid file with old contents of the sector nothing: the data is simply wrong

The third case is the dangerous one: the next file created on the disk can be given the same cluster, and then two files share it, the cross-link of Lab 7.4. Nothing on the disk records that the volume was in use when the power failed, so CHKDSK must be run by hand; until then MS-DOS uses the inconsistent FAT.

UFS2 with soft updates. Creating /mnt/new changes the inode bitmap of a cylinder group, the new inode, the directory block of /mnt, the directory's inode (size and times), and for data the block bitmap and the data block. Soft updates enforce three rules (McKusick and Ganger's paper, see Further reading): never point to a structure before it has been initialised (the inode is written before the directory entry that names it), never reuse a resource before all pointers to it are gone, and never reset the last pointer to a live resource before a new one is set. When the directory block must be written while the new inode is still only in memory, the softdep code rolls back the new entry in the copy being written (Listing 7.18) and rolls it forward after the write. Whatever subset of the writes reaches the disk, the result is either the old state or the old state plus allocated-but-unreferenced inodes and blocks. Those leaks are harmless: the file system can be mounted at once, and fsck_ffs reclaims them later in the background, on a snapshot of the running file system. With SU+J, the journal records the pending operations, and fsck_ffs replays it in seconds instead of scanning every cylinder group.

What to notice. Both systems write metadata asynchronously for speed. MS-DOS accepts any order and repairs afterwards, with a tool that cannot always know the right answer (which file owns a cross-linked cluster?). FreeBSD constrains the order so that the only possible damage is the one that is safe to repair automatically. Neither protects the contents of a file being written: an application that needs that calls fsync(2) on FreeBSD or INT 21h function 68h ("commit file") on MS-DOS 4.00 ($Commit, entry 68h of the dispatch table, MS_TABLE.ASM line 403).

Discussion questions.

  1. On FAT, which single change to the order of writes would make the dangerous third case impossible? What would it cost?
  2. Why can fsck_ffs run in the background on a mounted soft-updates file system but CHKDSK /F cannot safely run while other programs write to the disk? (Think about what CHKDSK reads with INT 25h.)
  3. A UFS2 file system without soft updates or journaling (newfs -u) mounted with -o async behaves in a crash like FAT. Why would anyone choose that?

Study case 7.C: Looking up a name in a directory#

Goal. Compare how both systems find NOTES.TXT in a directory, and what it costs in a large directory.

MS-DOS. SEARCH (DIR.ASM lines 86-140) reads the directory one sector at a time through the buffers (16 entries per 512-byte sector), compares the 11 bytes of each entry with the name in NAME1 using MetaCompare (which also handles ? wildcards), skips free (E5h) entries, and stops at the first 00h byte. The root directory of a 1.44 MB disk is at most 14 sectors; a subdirectory can grow, and a lookup in a directory with 2,000 files reads up to 125 sectors and compares up to 2,000 names. Every path component repeats this, and the kernel has no name cache: FASTOPEN, an optional resident program in 4.00, caches recently found names and their clusters for that reason.

FreeBSD. ufs_lookup first consults the system-wide name cache (namecache, used for every file system), and only on a miss searches the directory. For a directory of 5 or more 512-byte chunks (ufs_mindirhashsize, ufs_dirhash.c lines 70-73) the first lookup builds an in-memory hash table of all its names, dirhash, and later lookups use it:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 7.26 – ufs_lookup tries the dirhash table before the linear scan (ufs_lookup.c lines 273-310)Source ↗
#ifdef UFS_DIRHASH
        /*
         * Use dirhash for fast operations on large directories. The logic
         * to determine whether to hash the directory is contained within
         * ufsdirhash_build(); a zero return means that it decided to hash
         * this directory and it successfully built up the hash table.
         */
        if (ufsdirhash_build(dp) == 0) {
                /* Look for a free slot if needed. */
                enduseful = dp->i_size;
                if (slotstatus != FOUND) {
                        slotoffset = ufsdirhash_findfree(dp, slotneeded,
                            &slotsize);
                        if (slotoffset >= 0) {
                                slotstatus = COMPACT;
                                enduseful = ufsdirhash_enduseful(dp);
                                if (enduseful < 0)
                                        enduseful = dp->i_size;
                        }
                }
                /* Look up the component. */
                numdirpasses = 1;
                entryoffsetinblock = 0; /* silence compiler warning */
                switch (ufsdirhash_lookup(dp, cnp->cn_nameptr, cnp->cn_namelen,
                    &i_offset, &bp, nameiop == DELETE ? &prevoff : NULL)) {
                case 0:
                        ep = (struct direct *)((char *)bp->b_data +
                            (i_offset & bmask));
                        goto foundentry;
                case ENOENT:
                        i_offset = roundup2(dp->i_size, DIRBLKSIZ);
                        goto notfound;
                default:
                        /* Something failed; just do a linear search. */
                        break;
                }
        }
#endif /* UFS_DIRHASH */

UFS_DIRHASH is in the GENERIC kernel ("Improve performance on big directories", GENERIC lines 44-48). The table is not stored on disk: the format stays the simple variable-length list of Listing 7.16, and the hash is rebuilt after a reboot or when memory is short.

What to notice. Both on-disk formats are unsorted lists, and both systems scan them linearly in the basic case. The difference is in memory: FreeBSD has a general name cache and a per-directory hash, MS-DOS has 20 sector buffers and an optional add-on. On a 1988 PC with 640 KB, memory for a hash of every large directory was simply not available; on a modern machine it is cheap.

Discussion questions.

  1. Estimate the number of sectors MS-DOS reads to open \DOS\UTIL\SUB\FILE.TXT when each directory has 300 entries and none is in a buffer. How many does FreeBSD read the second time?
  2. Why does UFS keep DIRBLKSIZ at 512 bytes even though blocks are 32 KB?
  3. Neither format keeps directories sorted. Name a file system that does, and the cost of doing so.

Homework#

Hand in source code, transcripts and answers as one archive. Cite the source lines (permalinks) that support every explanation. MS-DOS programs must be run on the MS-DOS 4.00 lab system with dos_run.py or dosb.py, with the output included.

Exercise 7.1: Writing a file into a FAT image#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 4 h.

Extend fatx.py with a put LOCALFILE [DOSPATH] command that copies a file from your computer into a FAT12 or FAT16 image, in the root directory or in an existing subdirectory, and an rm DOSPATH command.

  • Allocate clusters from the FAT, link them, write the chain into every FAT copy, write the data, and create a directory entry with the archive attribute, the file's modification time packed as in DIRENT.INC, the first cluster and the size.
  • Choose and justify an order for the three kinds of writes (Study case 7.B).
  • Verify on MS-DOS 4.00: put the image in B: with dosb.py and run CHKDSK B:, CHKDSK B:*.*, DIR and FC /B against the original file (copied to A: with --file). CHKDSK must report no errors.
  • Test a file that does not fit in the first hole of the disk (it must be fragmented), an empty file, and a full root directory.

Deliverables: the program, the dosb.py transcripts, a paragraph on your write order.

Hints: Volume.set_fat already packs FAT12 entries in all copies; Volume.dir_slots gives you the slots of a directory. A free slot starts with 00h or E5h. Do not grow a subdirectory in a first version.

Exercise 7.2: How big can it get?#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 2 h.

From the structures, compute and justify with permalinks:

  1. The maximum number of clusters of a FAT12 and of a FAT16 volume in MS-DOS 4.00 (use the threshold of Module 2, section 2.4, and the reserved values of Listing 2.19).
  2. The maximum volume size for FAT12 with the cluster sizes of DISKTABLE (MSINIT.ASM lines 262-268) and for FAT16 with each row of Listing 7.9, and the maximum file size on FAT16 (two limits: the size field and the volume).
  3. The maximum file size of UFS2 with 4 KB, 16 KB and 32 KB blocks, using mkfs.c lines 311-315 and NINDIR = block size / 8. Check the 32 KB value against fs_maxfilesize in Output 7.5.
  4. The largest UFS2 file system: what limits it, fs_size (64 bits, in fragments) or something else?

Deliverables: a table and the arithmetic.

Exercise 7.3: BOOTINFO in assembly#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write BOOTINFO.COM (NASM, org 100h) that reads sector 0 of a drive given on the command line (default: the current drive) with INT 25h in the DOS 4.00 form (CX = -1, packet with a 32-bit sector number, Listing 7.8 and ABS_32RW in DEVSYM.INC lines 171-175), and prints the OEM name, the BPB fields, the media byte and, if the extended boot signature 29h is present, the 32-bit total, the serial number, the label and the file system id.

  • Remember that INT 25h leaves the flags on the stack.
  • Run it on A: and on a data diskette in B: formatted by FORMAT (Lab 7.3), and on a drive letter that does not exist.
  • Compare the serial number with DIR's and explain the byte order.

Deliverables: source, transcript, a one-paragraph explanation of the serial number's byte order.

Exercise 7.4: Reading a superblock in C on FreeBSD#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write sbinfo.c for FreeBSD that opens a device or an image, reads the superblock with pread(2) at SBLOCK_UFS2 into a struct fs from <ufs/ffs/fs.h>, checks the magic number and prints block and fragment size, number of cylinder groups, inodes per group, free blocks, fragments and inodes, the flags (soft updates, journal) and fs_maxfilesize. Then locate the root inode with the macros ino_to_fsba, ino_to_fsbo and fsbtodb of fs.h (Listing 7.13) and print its mode, link count, size and first block.

  • Run it on the memory disk of Lab 7.5 (attached again from /tmp/ufs32.img), before and after tunefs -j enable, on the image file /tmp/ufs32.img itself, and on the VM's root partition.
  • Compare every value with dumpfs and with ufsx.py.

Deliverables: source, transcripts, the comparison.

Hints: an image file can be read at any offset and in any length, a disk device cannot: GEOM rejects a transfer that does not start on a sector boundary or is not a whole number of sectors long, with EINVAL (geom_io.c lines 443-448). Read the superblock with SBLOCKSIZE bytes and the inode with the whole block that holds it, as the kernel does. After tunefs -j enable, look at the size of the root directory.

Exercise 7.5: The DPB from C on MS-DOS#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write DPBINFO.C for Microsoft C 5.10 (build it with tools/dos_tools.py, CL /AS DPBINFO.C) that calls INT 21h function 32h ($GET_DPB, MISC.ASM lines 161-203) with intdosx, and prints every field of the DPB of Listing 7.1 with its meaning. Declare the DPB as a packed struct (careful: dpb_FAT_size became a word in 4.00).

  • Run it for A: and B: from the command line, and from a batch file on B: that runs DPBINFO, then COPY K1.DAT NEW.DAT, then DPBINFO again. Explain why dpb_next_free is 0 in the first runs and not in the second (Lab 7.3).
  • Explain why function 32h itself may reset the cursor (read the comment "Force Media Check").

Deliverables: source, transcripts, the explanation.

Hints: in the small model, FP_SEG and FP_OFF need an lvalue that is a near variable holding a far pointer; copy a far pointer field into a local variable first.

Exercise 7.6: Fragmentation on UFS2#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2 h.

Write frag.sh, the FreeBSD counterpart of FRAG.BAT: on a 32 MB memory disk with a fresh UFS2 file system, create three 32 KB files, delete the middle one, append 32 KB to the first, create a fourth, and print the block list of every file with fsdb -r (inode N, blocks; fsdb -r refuses cd, Lab 7.5). Explain the layout with ffs_alloc and ffs_blkpref_ufs2 (Listing 7.17 and its neighbours), and compare it with Lab 7.3. Then add a sync right after the rm and run the script again: what changes, and why?

Deliverables: the script, its output, a half-page comparison.

Exercise 7.7: Essay: why FAT survived#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2 h.

FAT was designed for floppies of a few hundred kilobytes, yet in 2026 it is still on every EFI system partition (Output 7.1), on SD cards in cameras and on USB sticks, while UFS, technically far ahead since 1984, stayed on BSD systems. In 800-1,000 words, explain why. Use at least four arguments from this module (size and simplicity of the format, what the metadata does not contain, crash behaviour, the cost of an implementation in firmware, compatibility across operating systems), and cite at least four source lines from either system.

Further reading#

  • Marshall Kirk McKusick, William N. Joy, Samuel J. Leffler, Robert S. Fabry, "A Fast File System for UNIX", ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2(3), 1984: the design of FFS and its cylinder groups.
  • Marshall Kirk McKusick and Gregory R. Ganger, "Soft Updates: A Technique for Eliminating Most Synchronous Writes in the Fast Filesystem", Proceedings of the FREENIX Track, USENIX Annual Technical Conference, 1999; and McKusick and Jeffery Roberson, "Journaled Soft-updates", BSDCan 2010.
  • Marshall Kirk McKusick, George V. Neville-Neil and Robert N. M. Watson, The Design and Implementation of the FreeBSD Operating System, 2nd edition, Addison-Wesley, 2014: chapters on the local file store and GEOM.
  • The FreeBSD manual pages in build/freebsd/root/usr/share/man: fs(5), ffs(4), newfs(8), dumpfs(8), fsdb(8), fsck_ffs(8), tunefs(8), mdconfig(8), md(4), gpart(8), geom(8), diskinfo(8), mount_msdosfs(8), msdosfs(4).
  • Ray Duncan (ed.), The MS-DOS Encyclopedia, Microsoft Press, 1988: the FAT format, INT 25h/26h and the device driver interface as documented for versions 1.0 through 3.2 (the book predates 4.00).
  • Microsoft, Microsoft Extensible Firmware Initiative FAT32 File System Specification, version 1.03, 2000: the later history of the format (FAT32, long names) that MS-DOS 4.00 predates.
